young.note: a dense rounded young tree, leafy to the ground, smooth grey bark

description: The broad evergreen oak of the coastal hills, often wider than it is tall, its limbs sweeping out low from a short trunk. Its small, stiff, cupped leaves are dark and shiny above and prickle at the edges.

season_notes.winter: Dark and glossy through the rains, the one green crown on many open slopes.
season_notes.spring: A flush of bright yellow-green new leaves and hanging catkins covers the old dark foliage in March and April.
season_notes.summer: The dense dome throws the deepest shade on the hills; old leaves yellow and drop.
season_notes.fall: Slender pointed acorns ripen in a single year and fall, drawing jays, squirrels and deer.

range.where: coastal hills, canyon bottoms and north slopes from Mendocino to Baja California; the oak woodland of San Francisco, Marin and the Peninsula

notes: Grown from interior live oak, its close relative and look-alike, with a broader, lower dome (FEIS: open-grown crowns broad and dense, often reaching the ground) and darker leaves. The leaves are convex, cupped like a shallow spoon, with hair tufts in the vein axils beneath (Jepson key, via SDSU), which separates it from interior live oak's flat leaves; at a distance the crown reads darker and glossier. The generator cannot draw the cupping or the gloss beyond the elliptic_glossy card. Bark: FEIS gives the thickest bark of the California oaks, smooth and grey when young, deeply furrowed with age; old coastal trees are also wind-pruned, which the higher asymmetry only hints at. Acorn eaters from FEIS (scrub jays and acorn woodpeckers take over half their fall and winter diet in acorns; ground squirrels and jays cache them); deer browse sprouts and foliage. Dusky-footed woodrats and yellow-billed magpies use it too but are not in the animal library. Wild turkeys are listed because the library has them, though they are introduced here.
